body_markdown:
This hub answers 24 of the most frequently asked questions about payroll and HR service costs. Organized into five sections, Pricing Fundamentals, Vendor-by-Vendor Costs, Service Tier Comparison, Add-Ons and Hidden Fees, and Choosing the Right Model, these answers give growth-stage operators the cost clarity they need to select a compliant, budget-aligned payroll solution. Every figure below is compiled from published vendor pricing and third-party pricing trackers as of August 2026; several of these vendors, Asure among them, price by custom quote instead of a fixed public rate, so confirm current numbers directly with each vendor before budgeting against them.


## Pricing Fundamentals


### What is the average cost of payroll services for a small business?


Most small businesses running standalone payroll software pay somewhere between $150 and $600 a month, depending on headcount and feature tier, typically working out to $6 to $12 per employee on top of a base platform fee. That range sits far below a PEO's typical per-employee cost, often 10 to 25 times higher per employee once the PEO's bundled HR and benefits administration are factored in, since a PEO prices as a percentage of payroll or a flat per-employee rate that covers considerably more than payroll processing alone. That gap is the reason a straight dollar comparison between a standalone payroll platform and a PEO rarely tells the whole story: the PEO's higher number is buying benefits access, HR administration, and often workers' compensation coverage bundled in on top of payroll itself, a meaningfully broader scope of work than a payroll platform's monthly fee covers alone. Managed services that aren't structured as a PEO, AsureWorks among them, price differently for exactly this reason: since they don't require the co-employment or bundled-benefits structure a PEO does, the number reflects the scope of payroll and HR administration actually being handed off rather than a full PEO package, worth knowing before assuming every managed option carries PEO-level pricing.


### What is the difference between self-managed, hybrid, and fully managed payroll?


Self-managed means the employer runs payroll on a software platform themselves, with Gusto's core plans and AsureCentral both common examples of that self-service model. Fully managed means a provider's specialists run payroll on the employer's behalf. The classic version of this is a PEO, which requires a co-employment arrangement, but it isn't the only fully managed option: AsureWorks is built specifically as a PEO alternative, Asure's specialists handle payroll and day-to-day HR administration directly, with no co-employment structure, so the employer remains the employer of record throughout. Hybrid sits between the two: software-led with expert support layered on top when needed, short of a full hand-off of execution. The cost gap between these three models is usually the single largest lever in a payroll budget, well before any vendor-specific pricing comparison matters.


### Is there a payroll solution with no monthly base fee?


Yes, for a specific use case. Square Payroll's contractor-only plan charges $6 per contractor paid, with no monthly base fee at all, covering unlimited pay runs and 1099 filings. It does not cover W-2 employees or automated tax filings for a W-2 workforce, so it fits a business paying only 1099 contractors specifically. A company with even one W-2 employee alongside its contractors needs the full W-2 plan, which does carry a base fee, so the zero-base advantage disappears the moment a single employee moves onto payroll rather than being paid as a contractor. For a company that's already outgrowing a contractor-only structure, or running a mix of W-2 employees and contractors from the outset, AsureCentral prices as a standard monthly-plus-per-employee platform rather than a contractor-only flat rate, and AsureWorks is worth a look if handing that W-2 payroll off entirely, rather than running it in-house, fits better.


## Vendor-by-Vendor Costs


### How much does AsureCentral or AsureWorks cost?


Like several other vendors in this comparison, Paycor, Paycom, Paylocity, and Ceridian Dayforce among them, Asure prices AsureCentral and AsureWorks by custom quote instead of a published flat rate, based on headcount, the specific modules needed, and which service model fits: AsureCentral for a company running payroll and HR itself with software support, or AsureWorks for a company that wants Asure's specialists handling payroll and day-to-day HR administration directly, without the co-employment structure a PEO requires, so the company stays the employer of record throughout. Comparable software-led small-business payroll and HR platforms in this same range typically run somewhere around $30 to $60 a month plus $4 to $8 per employee for core payroll and HR, a reasonable ballpark for AsureCentral specifically, though AsureWorks' fully managed pricing depends more on the scope of HR administration handed off than any fixed per-employee number, and Asure's own quote is the only way to confirm an exact figure for a specific headcount and module mix. That quote-based approach isn't unique to Asure in this list, and it reflects the same reality driving most of the higher-complexity vendors covered elsewhere in this comparison: a fixed per-employee number rarely captures what a specific company's actual module mix and service level end up costing, which is exactly why so many of the vendors on this page, not just Asure, have moved away from publishing a flat rate card at all.


### How much does ADP cost per month for small businesses?


RUN Powered by ADP's entry-level Essential plan starts at roughly $79 a month plus about $4 per employee, though ADP quotes final pricing individually based on headcount, pay frequency, states of operation, and features needed. Most small businesses running RUN end up paying somewhere between $100 and $300 a month total once the per-employee fee and any add-ons are factored in.


### How much does Paychex cost per month?


Paychex Flex Essentials publishes a starting rate of $39 a month plus $5 per employee. Paychex's higher tiers, Select and Pro, skip a published rate card entirely and are priced by custom quote, so the specific monthly figure for those tiers depends on the deal negotiated. Worth knowing if you're comparing Paychex against Paycor specifically: Paychex completed a $4.1 billion acquisition of Paycor in April 2025, so the two are no longer fully independent competitors the way they were when most existing comparison content was written.


### How much does Gusto cost monthly?


Gusto's Simple plan runs $49 a month plus $6 per employee, Plus runs $80 a month plus $12 per employee, and Premium runs $180 a month plus $22 per employee, all as of a March 2026 price adjustment that raised the entry-level Simple plan from its prior $40 base. A contractor-only plan is also available at $35 a month plus $6 per contractor, similar in structure to Square's contractor-only option but with a base fee Square's plan doesn't carry.


### How much does QuickBooks payroll cost per month?


QuickBooks Payroll's Core plan runs about $44 a month, with a Premium and Plus bundle around $101.50 a month, plus a per-employee fee that generally runs $6 to $10 depending on tier. Pricing here is worth double-checking against whatever figure you find elsewhere: Intuit raised QuickBooks pricing roughly 20 to 25 percent across its tiers during 2026, so older comparison content, including tier names and figures that may still reference a separate "Elite" tier, is likely to understate the current cost. Some of that current pricing also reflects a limited-time promotional discount on the first few months, so the number a new customer sees at signup can look noticeably lower than the standard rate that applies once the promotional window ends.


### How much does Square Payroll cost per month?


For a W-2 workforce, Square Payroll charges a monthly base fee plus a per-employee fee, in the same general range as Gusto's and QuickBooks's entry tiers. For contractors only, there is no base fee at all, just $6 per contractor paid in a given month, a flat, straightforward rate built specifically for a contractor-only workforce.


### How much does BambooHR cost per month?


BambooHR's Core, Pro, and Elite tiers run roughly $10, $17, and $25 per employee per month respectively, with a $250-a-month floor that applies to any team under about 25 employees regardless of which tier is selected. Payroll itself is a separate add-on, estimated at $6 to $8 per employee per month on top of the base HR platform fee, which means a typical small team's all-in monthly total, HR platform plus payroll add-on, often lands somewhere between $200 and $900 depending on headcount and tier.


### How much does Paycor cost per month?


Paycor's four published tiers historically ran Basic at $99 a month plus $5 per employee, Essential at $149 a month plus $7, Core at $199 a month plus $8, and Complete at $199 a month plus $14. Paycor pulled its public pricing page in 2025 and now quotes every deal individually, so those figures serve as a historical reference point, not a current rate card; third-party buyer-reported contract data puts real-world annual Paycor spend anywhere from roughly $6,300 to $56,000 depending on company size and modules, a wide enough range that the published tier figures above are mostly useful for understanding Paycor's general structure rather than predicting an actual quote.


### How much does Paycom cost per month?


Paycom's full HCM platform runs roughly $25 to $35 per employee per month depending on headcount and add-ons, while payroll-only service runs about half that, roughly $12 to $18 per employee per month. Paycom also charges a one-time implementation fee on top, commonly cited at 30 to 35 percent of the first year's subscription cost, worth factoring into any first-year budget comparison against a vendor with a lower or no implementation fee. That implementation fee alone can meaningfully change which vendor actually costs less in year one specifically, even when two vendors' ongoing per-employee rates look nearly identical on paper.


### How much does Paylocity cost per month?


Paylocity's full HCM suite runs roughly $26 to $33 per employee per month, with core HR and payroll alone starting closer to $5 per employee per month before add-ons. Paylocity does not publish pricing and quotes every deal individually, with mid-market buyers in the 200 to 500 employee range commonly reporting all-in per-employee rates in the mid-teens to low twenties once their specific module mix is priced.


### How much does Ceridian Dayforce cost per month?


Estimates for Dayforce's core payroll and HCM run roughly $22 to $31 per employee per month, though third-party estimates range as low as $10 to $25 depending on which modules are included, since Dayforce prices in capability tiers, a base tier plus separate add-on modules for time and attendance, benefits, talent, and workforce management, each adding its own per-employee charge. For context at scale, a 1,000-employee company has been reported paying somewhere in the range of $22,000 to $45,000 a month in software fees alone, before implementation, which industry sources put at 40 to 60 percent of the annual software fee. That implementation figure alone can run into six figures for a company at this scale, a cost most smaller-headcount comparisons on this page don't need to think about at all, which is part of why Dayforce is generally positioned toward larger, more complex organizations than most of the other vendors in this comparison.


### How much does Zenefits (TriNet HR Platform) cost per month?


TriNet's HR Platform, the product formerly branded Zenefits, has historically published Essentials, Growth, and Zen tiers around $8, $16, and $21 per employee per month respectively, with a payroll add-on around $6 per employee per month and an HR advisory add-on around $8 per employee per month on top. The Zenefits-to-TriNet brand transition has introduced some pricing variation across sources, so confirming a current quote directly is worth doing before budgeting against any of these historical figures. Stacking the base tier, the payroll add-on, and the HR advisory add-on together at the entry Essentials tier puts a rough all-in estimate around $22 per employee per month before any other module is added, a useful starting point for comparing against the bundled HR-plus-payroll platforms elsewhere on this page, since the base tier figure on its own understates what most buyers actually end up paying.


## Service Tier Comparison


### What does a fully managed payroll or PEO service cost per month?


Fully managed and PEO pricing typically runs $150 to $200 per employee per month, or 2 to 12 percent of total payroll, depending on the provider and the scope of services bundled in. For a 25-person company, that works out to roughly $3,750 to $5,000 a month, a materially different cost magnitude than any of the self-managed software platforms above, since a PEO's price covers benefits administration, HR support, and often workers' compensation alongside payroll itself. AsureWorks is a specific example of a managed service that isn't a PEO: Asure's specialists run payroll and HR administration directly, without the co-employment structure a PEO requires, so pricing reflects the scope of work actually handed off rather than a bundled PEO package. That kind of managed service, non-PEO but still fully hands-off, can sit at a meaningfully different price point than either the pure-software platforms above or the full PEO figure here, since the service scope and the underlying delivery model both affect the number more than the label "managed" does on its own.


### How does Gusto's pricing compare to QuickBooks payroll for a 10-person company?


At 10 employees, Gusto's Simple plan runs about $109 a month, while QuickBooks Core runs somewhat higher once its 2026 pricing increase is factored in. Both sit in a similar entry-level band for a small, straightforward payroll, and the more consequential difference between them tends to be feature depth and integration fit, particularly if the business already runs its bookkeeping through QuickBooks, well beyond whatever narrow dollar gap separates them at this specific headcount. For a 10-person company weighing more than a bare payroll platform, AsureCentral is worth a quote at this same headcount, since it isn't scoped only to larger companies the way some of the quote-based platforms elsewhere in this comparison are, and it brings payroll, HR, and compliance onto one connected system rather than pairing a payroll tool with separate bookkeeping software.


### Does ADP charge processing fees on top of the monthly base?


Yes, on top of the base plan and per-employee fee, ADP has historically charged separate per-run processing fees in the range of $25 to $75, which adds up meaningfully across a standard biweekly schedule: 26 pay runs a year at that range works out to roughly $650 to $1,950 a year in processing fees alone, before the base subscription and per-employee charges are even added in. Confirm current per-run fees directly with ADP, since this is exactly the kind of add-on charge that varies by plan and negotiated contract. This category of fee is worth checking against every vendor in this comparison equally, since a per-run processing charge that doesn't appear in a headline monthly rate can shift the real annual cost comparison between two vendors that otherwise look similarly priced on paper.


## Add-Ons and Hidden Fees


### What are the typical add-on fees that increase payroll costs?


The most common add-ons across these vendors are W-2 or 1099 form fees, often $50 to $200 or more depending on filing volume, off-cycle payroll run fees in the $25 to $75 range, and garnishment processing fees of roughly $5 to $15 per pay period per garnishment. Stacked together, these add-ons commonly inflate a quoted base price by 20 to 40 percent once a full year of actual usage is factored in, which is why a quoted monthly rate rarely matches the total annual cost a business actually pays. A company that runs one off-cycle payroll a quarter, issues a handful of garnishments, and files standard W-2s at year-end can easily add several hundred dollars a year on top of the advertised base and per-employee rate, purely from these three add-on categories combined. A connected platform where payroll, time, and HR data all live in one system, the architecture AsureCentral is built around, can reduce how often some of these add-ons get triggered in the first place, since fewer off-cycle runs and manual corrections are needed when hours and employee changes flow directly into payroll instead of being re-entered by hand.


### What hidden costs should I watch for when comparing payroll vendors?


Setup or implementation fees ranging from $0 to $500 or more, phone support that's restricted or unavailable below a certain plan tier, and per-run or per-form charges that don't show up in a headline monthly rate are the most common gaps between a quoted price and an actual bill. A vendor that advertises phone support prominently on its marketing page can still restrict it to a higher tier than the plan a small business actually signs up for, which only becomes apparent the first time an urgent payroll problem needs a live person instead of a support ticket queue. Requesting a full, itemized fee schedule in writing before signing is the single most reliable way to catch these before they show up on an invoice; the advertised base rate alone almost never covers the full picture. Platform visibility helps too: Luna AI, embedded across AsureCentral, is built to flag payroll exceptions and unusual charges as a pay run happens rather than leaving them to surface only once a monthly invoice arrives, a different kind of protection than a fee schedule provides but aimed at the same underlying problem, costs that hide until it's too late to catch them easily.


### Can I negotiate payroll vendor pricing?


Often, yes, particularly at 25 or more employees or when committing to a 12-month or longer contract. Waived setup fees, complimentary W-2 filing, and discounted add-on pricing are the concessions most commonly available, though how much room there is to negotiate depends heavily on headcount and the specific vendor's current sales incentives, so results vary more than a fixed negotiation playbook would suggest. Asking directly whether a longer initial term unlocks a lower effective rate, and getting any verbal concession written into the contract itself, matters more than the specific ask, since a discount promised during a sales call carries little weight if it never makes it into the signed agreement. This applies directly to Asure's own pricing too: since AsureCentral and AsureWorks are priced by custom quote rather than a fixed rate card, the module mix, contract length, and headcount discussed during that quote conversation are exactly where the effective rate gets set, the same dynamic at play with the other custom-quote vendors in this comparison.


## Choosing the Right Model


### How much does an AsureWorks-managed model cost compared to running payroll on a self-service platform like Gusto or QuickBooks?


There's no fixed dollar comparison here because the two models solve different problems: a self-service platform charges for software access and expects the employer's own team to run payroll, while AsureWorks charges for Asure's specialists to run payroll and day-to-day HR administration directly, without the co-employment structure of a PEO, so the employer remains the employer of record throughout. The right comparison isn't which number is smaller, it's whether a growth-stage company has the internal capacity to run payroll accurately itself or would rather have that operational work handled by someone else while keeping full control of workforce decisions. A company weighing this decision purely on the self-service platform's advertised monthly rate is comparing a partial number against a fuller one: the self-service rate covers software access alone, while the managed-service rate covers the labor of actually running payroll correctly each cycle, a cost that shows up somewhere in a self-service model too, usually as internal staff time that never appears on an invoice.


### How do I choose between ADP and Paychex for my business?


At small headcounts, the cost delta between ADP and Paychex is usually modest, often $10 to $30 a month at the entry tier, which means the decision more often comes down to support model and feature fit than price alone. ADP tends to fit a company anticipating growth into more complex, multi-state payroll, while Paychex has historically positioned its support toward businesses under about 50 employees, though that distinction is worth re-confirming given Paychex's 2025 acquisition of Paycor, since the combined company's positioning may shift over time. A company already leaning toward Paycor's specific feature set has a related question worth asking directly of a sales representative from either company: how the Paychex-Paycor combination affects long-term product roadmap and support continuity for whichever platform is ultimately selected, since an acquisition of this size rarely leaves both product lines completely unchanged over a multi-year contract term. Worth adding to that same shortlist: AsureCentral and AsureWorks are a legitimate third path at this decision point too, particularly for a company that wants the option to start self-service and move to a fully managed model later without switching platforms or vendors, an option neither ADP nor Paychex offers within one account the same way.


## Learn More


Payroll and HR service costs vary by a factor of ten or more depending on vendor, headcount, and service model, and a quoted base rate rarely reflects what a business actually pays once add-ons, processing fees, and implementation costs are factored in. AsureCentral and AsureWorks are legitimate, quote-based answers to the real decision sitting underneath every vendor in this comparison, ADP, Paychex, Gusto, QuickBooks, and the rest included: whether to run payroll and HR yourself on a self-service platform, or hand the operational work to a managed service instead. AsureCentral is built for a company that wants to run payroll and HR itself with a connected system of record and Luna AI built into the workflow, and AsureWorks is built for a company that wants Asure's specialists running payroll and day-to-day HR administration directly, without a PEO's co-employment structure, so the company remains the employer of record throughout, same platform, choice of who does the work.


Ready to see an actual number instead of a published range? Request a quote for AsureCentral or AsureWorks directly from Asure and get a cost built around your specific headcount, states of operation, and service model, the same custom-quote conversation several of the vendors in this comparison require, but with the option to start self-service and move to fully managed later without switching platforms.
